title: Phones in School
resolution: Resolved: Schools should ban student cell phones for the entire school day.
summary: Most states now require schools to ban or restrict student phones. Should the ban cover the whole day, "bell to bell," including lunch and passing periods?

background.p: As of spring 2026, at least 37 states and the District of Columbia required school districts to ban or restrict student phone use, according to reporting by the Associated Press and The 74. Policies range from "off and away" during class to bell-to-bell bans in which phones are locked in pouches or lockers all day.

A large study published by the National Bureau of Economic Research in 2026, co-led by Stanford economist Thomas Dee and using data from about 4,600 schools that used lockable pouches, found average effects on test scores close to zero over the first three years. Suspensions rose about 16% in the first year and returned to normal by the third. Student well-being dipped in the first year and was above its starting level by the third. Teachers reported personal phone use in class falling from 61% to 13% under bell-to-bell bans.

positions: The largest U.S. study to date found average test-score effects close to zero in the first three years, with some newer schools seeing gains.
Supporters point to studies from other countries and to large drops in classroom phone use, and argue benefits may take time to appear.

terms.def: Phones are put away for the whole school day, including lunch and passing periods.
Phones must be silent and out of sight during class but may be used at other times.
A locking pouch students keep with them; it is unlocked at the end of the day.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: A full-day ban gives students hours of focus and face-to-face time that a class-only rule can't.

args.claim: A full-day ban cuts phone use far more than class-only rules.
args.warrant: When phones are allowed at lunch and between classes, students keep checking them, and notifications pull attention back into class. Locking them away removes the temptation.
args.evidence: The 2026 NBER study's teacher surveys (phone use in class fell from 61% to 13% under bell-to-bell bans); device-ping data dropping by about 30% by year three.
args.response: The negative answers that less phone use hasn't yet shown up as higher test scores, so the benefit is unproven.

args.warrant: Without the constant pull of social media during the day, students talk to each other more and face less online conflict at school.
args.evidence: The same study's finding that well-being dipped in year one but rose above baseline by year three; surveys of students and teachers in ban schools.
args.response: The negative points out that the first-year dip and rise in suspensions are real costs, and later gains may reflect other changes.

args.claim: Clear, simple rules are easier to enforce.
args.warrant: A class-only rule means teachers argue with students all day about whether a phone is out. One rule for the whole day removes the gray areas.
args.evidence: Teacher surveys and union statements supporting full-day policies; district reports on enforcement time.
args.response: The negative replies that the 2026 study found suspensions rose in the first year, so strict rules can also create more conflict.

args.claim: Schools can meet safety and family needs another way.
args.warrant: Parents can reach students through the school office, and students with medical needs can be given exceptions, so a full ban need not cut off emergencies.
args.evidence: State laws with exceptions for medical devices and emergencies; school emergency-communication plans.
args.response: The negative argues that in an emergency, parents want direct contact, and office lines can be overwhelmed.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Phones should be put away in class, but a full-day ban costs too much for too little proven gain.

args.claim: The evidence for full-day bans is not yet strong.
args.warrant: A rule affecting millions of students should show clear results. The largest U.S. study found test-score effects close to zero in the first three years.
args.evidence: The 2026 NBER study of about 4,600 schools (Dee and colleagues), as reported by AP and The 74.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the same study found big drops in phone use and later gains in well-being, and achievement effects may take longer.

args.claim: Families want to reach their children.
args.warrant: Parents use phones to coordinate rides, changes in plans and emergencies. Locking phones away all day removes that link.
args.evidence: Parent surveys on school phone policies; reports from districts debating emergency communication.
args.response: The affirmative replies that the school office and exceptions handle real needs, and that phones can distract students during an emergency.

args.claim: Teens need to learn to manage phones, not just be separated from them.
args.warrant: Adults must manage devices at work and home. Allowing phones at lunch while banning them in class teaches self-control that a total ban skips.
args.evidence: Digital-citizenship curricula; arguments from educators favoring class-only policies.
args.response: The affirmative answers that self-control is easier to learn with fewer temptations, and teens still have phones before and after school.

args.claim: Strict bans can raise discipline problems at first.
args.warrant: Enforcement creates confrontations, and suspensions take students out of class, which hurts learning.
args.evidence: The 2026 study's finding of a roughly 16% rise in suspensions in the first year.
args.response: The affirmative points out that the same study found the increase disappeared by the third year.

strawmen.strawman: Ban supporters think phones are evil and want to take them away from teenagers.
strawmen.why: Supporters focus on the school day, not on teens' phone use at home.
strawmen.steelman: During school hours, a simple full-day ban sharply cuts phone use and, over time, appears to improve student well-being.

strawmen.strawman: Opponents want kids scrolling social media during math class.
strawmen.why: Most opponents support putting phones away in class; they object to full-day bans.
strawmen.steelman: Class-time rules capture most of the benefit; a full-day ban adds costs for families and discipline without proven gains in learning.

weak.arg: Phone bans will raise test scores right away.
weak.why: The largest study found no average test-score effect in the first years. Claim what the evidence supports.
Schools provide laptops or tablets for schoolwork; personal phones aren't required for learning.
